clue.text: Did Mary's Spaniard long for these islands ?

definitions.note: plural islands for an adjective-style entry: the islands named after the Spanish king

parts.note: Mary I of England married Philip II of Spain
to long for something is to pine for it

explanation.surface: A question whether Queen Mary's Spanish husband was homesick for some faraway islands.
explanation.walkthrough: The islands were named after Philip II of Spain, husband of England's Mary Tudor, which makes the surface's history apt; the entry leaves off the final S.
explanation.definitionFit: The archipelago in the western Pacific takes its name from the Spanish king, and the entry is its adjective form.

clue.text: Lay up too much French wine

indicators.note: in a down clue, laying a word up sets its letters upwards, so it is read backwards

parts.note: trop is French for too much

explanation.surface: Advice not to cellar too much wine from France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lay up' reads as storing wine but means writing TROP (French for too much) upwards in the down column, giving the fortified wine.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong sweet fortified wine from Portugal.

clue.text: One horse there's no use troubling with — it's fiery

definitions.note: describes something as fiery; the answer is the adjective for it

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
a horse is a gee (gee-gee), and gee is the letter G

indicators.note: troubling the letters stirs them up into a new order

explanation.surface: A horse that is pointless to bother with, because it is hot-tempered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'troubling' signals the anagram of NO USE, giving NEOUS, after I and G (gee, a horse).
explanation.definitionFit: Rock formed by solidifying from molten magma is volcanic, born of fire.

clue.text: "Like sweet bells jangled" but unlike Milton's sphere-born sisters

definitions.meaning: Ophelia in Hamlet speaks of 'sweet bells jangled, out of tune and harsh'
Milton's 'At a Solemn Music' calls Voice and Verse 'sphere-born harmonious sisters'

explanation.surface: Two literary quotations compared: Shakespeare's discordant bells against Milton's musical sisters.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are literary: Ophelia's description of Hamlet's mind, and Milton's tuneful pair, whose epithet the answer negates.
explanation.definitionFit: Discordant and out of tune, as jangled bells are, and the opposite of Milton's melodious muses.

clue.text: Put forward in defence of sterling

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of
the pound is the unit of British sterling currency

explanation.surface: Arguments made in support of the British currency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put forward' looks like a description of the argument; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To propound a theory is to offer or advance it for consideration.

clue.text: A thousand and one dark reasons why a bride avoided being late

definitions.text: A thousand and one dark reasons why a bride avoided being late

parts.words: A thousand and one dark reasons why a bride avoided being late
parts.note: Scheherazade, the bride of the Arabian tales, escaped execution, becoming 'the late', by telling stories over a thousand and one evenings

explanation.surface: Excuses for a bride who would not arrive after the appointed time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being late' reads as unpunctual but means dead: Scheherazade's tales spun out over 1001 dark evenings saved her from execution.
explanation.definitionFit: Periods of darkness; the Arabian collection is named for the thousand and one evenings of storytelling.

clue.text: Something to take care of if the cap fits

definitions.text: Something to take care of if the cap fits

parts.note: c/o, short for care of, as on an envelope
taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice on looking after a hat, with a nod to the proverb 'if the cap fits, wear it'.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: a close-fitting cap is a thing to look after if it fits you, and the wordplay is the abbreviation for 'care of' followed by IF.
explanation.definitionFit: A coif is a close-fitting skullcap, the kind of headwear a wearer would keep if it fitted.

clue.text: Effective way to opt out of near disaster

indicators.note: a disaster leaves things wrecked, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A good way to escape from an impending catastrophe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disaster' signals an anagram of OPT and NEAR together.
explanation.definitionFit: Something operant is operative, producing an effect.

clue.text: Bird-man's propeller-management or nest-improvement ?

definitions.meaning: an aviator sets propeller blades edge-on to the airflow
to line one's nest with down, as in the idiom for enriching oneself

explanation.surface: Two kinds of bird business, one about an airman's propeller and one about a nest.
explanation.walkthrough: A bird-man is an old word for an airman, who turns propeller blades edge-on to reduce drag; lining one's nest is an idiom for getting rich.
explanation.definitionFit: Turning a propeller's blades edge-on to the wind, and lining a nest with plumage, are both done with the same verb.

clue.text: Act quickly to transfix

explanation.surface: An instruction to a performer to hurry through the scene and hold the audience spellbound.
explanation.definitionFit: To dash through a performance quickly is to rehearse it in summary; to pierce a body with a sword or spear is to skewer it.

clue.text: Divine creature from another age

indicators.note: the letters are taken out from within the words that follow

explanation.surface: A goddess said to come from some bygone era.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' tells you to take the answer out of 'another age', across the word break.
explanation.definitionFit: She is the queen of the Greek gods, wife of Zeus, so a goddess.

clue.text: For a long time topping for Bottom, we hear

indicators.note: we hear signals that the phrase is to be judged by its sound

parts.note: Bottom the weaver in A Midsummer Night's Dream is given an ass's head, with long asinine ears on top

explanation.surface: Bottom wears his ass's head for a long while, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's play Bottom is turned into an ass; the ears on his head sound like the British idiom meaning ages.
explanation.definitionFit: A British idiom meaning ages, a very long period.

clue.text: Doctor or uxoricide

parts.note: MO, medical officer, an army doctor
taken as written

explanation.surface: A puzzling choice between a physician and a wife-killer.
explanation.walkthrough: Othello, called the Moor of Venice in Shakespeare's play, smothers his wife Desdemona, so he is the wife-killer.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Othello, known by his North African origin, strangles his wife, so the title figure is a wife-slayer.

clue.text: Manipulator skilled in disc-jockeying ?

parts.note: the discs are those of the spine, and the jockeying is the practitioner's manipulation of them, not playing records

explanation.surface: A radio DJ praised for slick handling of records.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disc-jockeying' suggests a radio presenter; here the discs are spinal ones that a bone-manipulating therapist eases back into place.
explanation.definitionFit: A practitioner who treats ailments by manipulating bones and joints, notably the spinal column.

clue.text: Post-prandial feast treat, perhaps

definitions.note: an adjective for after a meal, describing the lingering flavour that the noun answer names

indicators.note: perhaps indicates the letters are one possible rearrangement

explanation.surface: A treat served after a dinner party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' signals an anagram of FEAST TREAT, and the result is what stays in the mouth after the meal.
explanation.definitionFit: The flavour lingering in the mouth once eating is over.

clue.text: Garlands of stones, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that these letters are only a possible arrangement, so they are reshuffled

explanation.surface: Decorative chains made out of pebbles, maybe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' signals an anagram of OF STONES.
explanation.definitionFit: Festoons are chains of flowers or ribbons hung in curves as decoration, that is, wreaths.

clue.text: Don't look to him to break the ice !

definitions.text: Don't look to him to break the ice !

parts.words: Don't look to him to break the ice !
parts.note: breaking the ice usually means easing a social silence, but here it is literal: someone gliding on a frozen pond hopes it holds

explanation.surface: A warning not to rely on a shy man to start conversation at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'break the ice' reads as starting a conversation; the person on blades over a frozen surface wants the ice to stay unbroken.
explanation.definitionFit: One who glides on blades over a frozen surface depends on the ice not cracking.

clue.text: Month Hood had no time for

definitions.text: Month Hood had no time for

parts.words: Month Hood had no time for
parts.note: Thomas Hood's poem lists everything missing from the late autumn, 'No sun, no moon... no birds', ending on the month's name

explanation.surface: Asking which month the man in the hood disliked.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Hood, an English poet, wrote 'No!', listing all the things the eleventh month lacks: its catalogue of 'no's ends with that month's name split as 'No-vember'.
explanation.definitionFit: The eleventh month, which Hood's poem 'No!' blames for having nothing pleasant.

clue.text: City hideout takes the cake

parts.note: EC is the postal district of the City of London
a lair is an animal's or criminal's hiding place

explanation.surface: A London bolt-hole that beats everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes the cake' looks like the idiom for being outrageous; 'takes' is just a link and 'the cake' the definition. The City is London's financial district, postcode EC.
explanation.definitionFit: An éclair is a finger-shaped choux pastry filled with cream and topped with chocolate.

clue.text: Dog has the staggers ?

definitions.meaning: a crossbred hunting dog, part greyhound

explanation.surface: A dog suffering from a staggering disease.
explanation.walkthrough: The dog is a British crossbreed, part sighthound; the second sense is one who reels, as in a horse disease called the staggers.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossbred sighthound used by poachers, and a person who reels unsteadily.

clue.text: A £25 coat ?

parts.note: a pony is British slang for twenty-five pounds
an animal's coat is its skin, here doubling as the defining word for the garment

explanation.surface: A question about a garment priced at twenty-five pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: In British betting slang a 'pony' is £25. The OCR dropped the pound sign.
explanation.definitionFit: A coat made from the hide of a small horse, a fur garment.

clue.text: A tinker changed to being a nail-maker

indicators.note: changed shows the letters are rearranged into something new

explanation.surface: A travelling metalworker who has turned into a nail manufacturer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changed' signals an anagram of A TINKER; 'nail-maker' looks like an ironmonger but means a protein that builds fingernails.
explanation.definitionFit: The fibrous protein that makes up hair, horns and fingernails.

clue.text: Boy and girl make woolly cloth

parts.note: Vic is a boy's name, short for Victor
Una is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A couple making a fabric together.
explanation.walkthrough: Two names, Vic and Una, side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Fabric woven from the fine wool of the South American camelid of that name.

clue.text: One of the setter's gems-we get ours quite out of the blue!

indicators.note: out of the blue means unexpectedly, as a wild jumble of letters arrives, so OURS QUITE is rearranged

explanation.surface: The setter boasts that a favourite jewel arrives quite unexpectedly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of the blue' signals the anagram of OURS QUITE, while hinting that the stone is itself sky-blue; it is December's birthstone, so perhaps the setter's.
explanation.definitionFit: An opaque sky-blue to green semi-precious stone, used in jewellery.

clue.text: The mayoress was this in service long ago

indicators.note: the answer is said to be what was contained inside the word that follows

explanation.surface: Recalling a lady mayor's past role as a domestic servant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'was this in' tells you the answer sits inside 'mayoress', in its middle letters.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Of yore' means in olden days, times past.

clue.text: Dry one, in a way

indicators.note: one letter placed inside the others

parts.note: RD, road
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A thirsty person in some fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a way' looks like 'somewhat'; it puts I inside A and RD (road). The printed (5) is a misprint for (4).
explanation.definitionFit: Arid land is parched, without moisture.

clue.text: One of the cries of London ?

definitions.text: One of the cries of London ?

parts.words: One of the cries of London ?
parts.note: the Cries of London were street-sellers' calls; here the cry is a hunting call that is also the name of a district of the West End

explanation.surface: A question about the traditional calls of London street-traders.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'cries of London' were street-sellers' shouts; the answer is an old hunting cry on sighting a hare, and also a district of central London.
explanation.definitionFit: A huntsman's halloo on spotting a hare, which is also the name of an area of the West End.

clue.text: Foolish fellow giving courses but not taking tips

definitions.text: Foolish fellow giving courses but not taking tips

parts.note: dumb means stupid
a waiter serves the courses of a meal

explanation.surface: A dim-witted waiter who brings the food but turns down gratuities.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes a small lift that carries dishes between kitchen and dining room: it delivers courses but, unlike a human server, gets no tips.
explanation.definitionFit: A small goods lift for carrying food between floors, which serves meals but is mute and unpaid.

clue.text: Cornish listeners

definitions.meaning: read as corn-ish: things of corn, the heads of the cereal plant

explanation.surface: People from Cornwall who pay attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cornish' looks like 'from Cornwall' (a county in south-west England); read as corn-ish it means the grain heads of corn.
explanation.definitionFit: Cereal plants carry their grain in heads called by the same word as the organs of hearing.

clue.text: Defended with troops, to gain orders another way

indicators.note: taking the letters another way means arranging them differently

explanation.surface: A military post manned to win commands by a different route.
explanation.walkthrough: 'another way' signals the anagram of GAIN ORDERS.
explanation.definitionFit: A fortified town supplied with a body of soldiers stationed to protect it.
